# The Heat Is Urban: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

When a heat wave strikes, the city itself becomes part of the problem. Asphalt absorbs sunlight all day and radiates it back at night, keeping temperatures several degrees higher than in surrounding countryside. This "urban heat island" effect is not an accident of geography; it is a design choice, made street by street and building by building over decades. The good news is that what was designed can be redesigned. Cities that take heat seriously—through trees, street design, housing standards, and public transit—can dramatically improve summer livability. But every intervention carries tradeoffs, and honest policy requires acknowledging them rather than pretending that cooling cities is free.

## Trees: The Oldest Air Conditioner

The single most effective tool against urban heat is also the oldest: shade. A mature street tree can lower the perceived temperature beneath its canopy by several degrees through shading alone, and by several more through evapotranspiration, the process by which leaves release water vapor. Studies in American cities have found that treeless neighborhoods can run five to ten degrees Fahrenheit hotter than leafy ones a few blocks away.
